title: Lookarounds at work
summary: Several rules at once with stacked lookaheads, lines that do not contain a word, what each tool and language supports, the commands seniors use, and thousands separators in one replace.

steps.title: Several lookaheads: all rules at once
body: Lookaheads at the start of a pattern all test from the same position, because none of them moves it. So a row
of them works as **and**:
```text
└ a digit   └ a lower   └ an upper  └ then: 12 or more non-space characters
Each `(?=.*X)` means "somewhere ahead there is an X". This is the classic interview pattern, and you will meet it
in existing sign-up forms and API token rules.
> **Tip:** for **new** password rules, current NIST guidance (SP 800-63B) says not to require character mixes:
> ask for length, and check the password against a list of breached ones. Use this technique for formats, such
> as tokens or ids that must contain certain parts.

steps.title: A token format rule
prompt: An internal API accepts a client secret only when the **whole** string has at least 12 characters, no whitespace,
and at least one ASCII digit, one lowercase and one uppercase letter, in any order. Write it with lookaheads.
hints: One lookahead per rule: `(?=.*[0-9])`, then the same for `[a-z]` and `[A-Z]`.
After the lookaheads, the part that actually consumes: `\S{12,}`. Anchor both ends.
steps.explain: Each lookahead scans ahead from the start and then returns there, so their order does not matter and adding a rule is one more `(?=...)`.

steps.title: Lines that do not contain a word
body: Regex has no "does not contain". A negative lookahead at the start of the line does the job:
```text
^(?!.*healthz).*$
At the start of each line, `(?!.*healthz)` looks ahead across the whole line. If `healthz` is anywhere, the line
fails. Otherwise `.*` takes it. The `.*` **inside** the lookahead matters: `^(?!healthz)` only checks the first
characters.
On the command line `grep -v healthz` is simpler. You need the regex form when a tool gives you a single pattern
field and no invert option: a log shipper's drop filter, an alert rule, an IDE search box.

steps.title: Drop the debug noise
prompt: The alerting tool takes one pattern to choose which lines to keep, applied with Multiline on. Keep every line
that does **not** contain `DEBUG` anywhere, whole line, one match per line.

all.input:
09:12 ERROR payment declined
09:12 DEBUG cache miss for user 42
09:13 WARN retry 2/5
09:13 api DEBUG: pool stats

hints: Start each line with a negative lookahead that scans the whole line: `(?!.*DEBUG)`.
steps.explain: `DEBUG` in the middle of the line is caught because the lookahead starts with `.*`. With `^(?!DEBUG)`, the fourth line would slip through.

steps.prompt: Where the `.*` goes matters. What does this print?
steps.explain: `(?!.*healthz)` looks across the whole line. `(?!healthz)` only checks whether the line **starts** with it, so the third line passes.

steps.title: Which engine supports what
body: Lookarounds are where flavours differ most. Know this before you copy a pattern between C#, a script and a terminal.
| Engine | Lookahead | Lookbehind |
| .NET (C#, PowerShell, Select-String) | yes | yes, any pattern |
| JavaScript (ES2018+, Node, browsers) | yes | yes, any pattern |
| Python `re` | yes | fixed width only: `(?<=\$)` works, `(?<=\$\s*)` is an error |
| PCRE2 (`grep -P`, `rg -P`, `git grep -P`, PHP) | yes | fixed width; PCRE2 10.43+ also allows a bounded length |
| Rust `regex` (plain `rg`), Go RE2 | **no** | **no** |
| POSIX (`grep -E`, `sed -E`, `awk`) | **no** | **no** |
Why Rust and Go leave them out: their engines guarantee linear time on any input, which rules out lookarounds and
backreferences. That is a security feature for patterns or input you do not control. In .NET,
`RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` makes the same trade: no lookarounds, no backreferences, linear time.
For Python, the third-party `regex` package allows variable-length lookbehind; or rewrite with a group and read it.

steps.prompt: Does this lookbehind work where it is used?
steps.explain: Fixed-width lookbehinds work almost everywhere that has lookarounds. Variable width works in .NET and JavaScript. Plain rg and POSIX grep have no lookarounds at all.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: lookarounds on the command line
steps.body: The default engines of rg and grep have no lookarounds, so seniors know which switch turns them on, and when inverting the search is simpler.

toolkit.what: Switch rg to the PCRE2 engine, which adds lookarounds and backreferences. Without -P, rg reports that lookaround is not supported.
flags: use PCRE2 instead of the default Rust engine
use the default engine, and PCRE2 only when the pattern needs it
toolkit.when: extracting a value by its context without printing the context

toolkit.what: GNU grep with PCRE. grep -E has no lookarounds. macOS ships BSD grep without -P: use rg -P or install GNU grep there.
toolkit.when: on Linux servers and in containers

toolkit.what: Invert the match: print the lines that do NOT match. Simpler and faster than a negative lookahead when the tool has the option.
flags: add a pattern; a line matching any of them is dropped
toolkit.example: kubectl logs deploy/api --since=10m | grep -v -e healthz -e readyz | grep -c ' 5[0-9][0-9] '
toolkit.when: cutting noise out of a log before you read it

toolkit.what: Search the tracked files of a repository (or any commit) with PCRE. Here: every blocking .Result on a Task, but not .ResultCode.
flags: PCRE (needs git built with PCRE, the default in most distributions)
search an older commit: git grep -P 'x' v1.4 -- src/
toolkit.when: code review and audits, including on old tags

toolkit.what: PowerShell uses the .NET engine, so every lookaround works, variable-length lookbehind included.
flags: every match on a line, not just the first
toolkit.when: on Windows, or when a pattern written for C# must run unchanged

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
pairs: print lines that do not match
PCRE search over the files tracked in a commit
PowerShell lines that do not match

steps.prompt: Complete the pipeline: from the API logs, drop the health checks, then print only the duration numbers that come after `duration=` and before `ms`.
steps.explain: `-v` inverts the first search, and `-P` switches the second rg to PCRE2 so the lookbehind and lookahead are allowed.

steps.title: Thousands separators in one replace
prompt: A support tool shows raw log text, and the team wants big numbers readable: `order 98765 of 100` should read
`order 98,765 of 100`. Write `string WithThousands(string text)` that inserts a comma into every run of digits,
every three digits counted from the right. Use **one** `Regex.Replace` that inserts `,` at the right positions, with no loop.
Build the position from three tests, all zero-width:
- `\B`: not at the edge of a word, so never before the first digit.
- `(?=(?:[0-9]{3})+...)`: followed by one or more groups of exactly three digits...
- `(?![0-9])`: ...after which no digit follows, so the groups reach the end of the number.
template: Dojo.Eq("numbers inside text", "order 98,765 of 100", WithThousands("order 98765 of 100"));
Dojo.Eq("short numbers stay", "3 of 42", WithThousands("3 of 42"));

forbid.message: No loop: the pattern finds the positions

hints: The pattern matches no characters at all, only positions, so the replacement `","` is inserted there.
steps.explain: Every match is empty, so `Replace` inserts without deleting. In review, ask what this does to `3.14159` (it gives `3.14,159`): when you hold an actual number, format it with `n.ToString("N0", culture)` instead, which also respects the reader's locale.
